cells.tense: You hold what your people handed you with steady hands, and you know the holding is yours.
cells.ask: Offer the thing you finished to the people who'll carry it next, and let them take it from you.
cells.core:
You keep what was handed down in working order, and it doesn't own you. You decide what to feed and what to let rest, what to carry forward and what to lay down. The care you keep here is the kind that doesn't exhaust or clutch. It just tends.

What's free to feed this is the moment a season ends. Passing something on not because you've run out but because it's complete — that's a different kind of giving, and the people who receive it can feel the difference. When what you've tended is finished, the exact right next move is to release it with both hands and let it land where it lands. You don't have to name it as letting go. But everybody around you can tell when the quiet work is done and you're still hovering. Finish the thing all the way, and give what's done the acknowledgment it's earned.
cells.sheetLine: You hold what was handed to you, and you let it go when it's done.
cells.verb: tending what grows with steady hands
cells.place: where a people keep what's worth passing on

cells.tense: You're already tending what hasn't sprouted yet, and you're tending it hard.
cells.ask: Let one thing fully run its course before you plant the next.
cells.core:
You know how to hold steady and you're using it on ground that hasn't been broken yet. You're bracing for a harvest before the soil's turned, tending crops that aren't yours to tend yet — and it's exhausting you. You're not controlling for the sake of control. You're trying to make the future arrive by holding it, and holding doesn't work that way. Connection holds better than any kind of grip. The spaces you try to fill ahead of time are spaces where people can still show up.

What's ahead matters enough to wait for. Let one thing run all the way through before you start the next one. Not planning it — living the next thing through to its actual end. When you let something finish, something in you finishes with it, and what comes after that is a fertile kind of rest. You don't have to know what the rest turns into. You just have to let the thing be over when it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending a harvest that hasn't been planted.
cells.verb: tending what grows with steady hands
cells.place: where a people keep what's worth passing on

cells.tense: You stopped nurturing what used to matter, and you can't remember the exact moment you put it down.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing you used to care for and give it ten minutes today.
cells.core:
Something you were tending got set down and never picked back up. It might have been a ritual, a practice, a craft, a person. It might have been yourself. The tending itself hasn't stopped being yours, but the part of you that started it is standing somewhere you've stopped reaching for. There's a wholeness waiting that doesn't require you to have it together first. You don't need to feel like it before you start. That's backwards, and waiting for the feeling first is what keeps this stuck.

Pick one small thing you used to tend, and give it ten minutes today. Not perfectly. Just tended. The wanting hasn't gone anywhere, and the act of tending something real is what brings the wanting back online. The point isn't the ten minutes. It's remembering that the caring part of you is still yours to pick up. No need to feel finished. Just start.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending what you love, and the wanting went quiet with it.

cells.tense: You're already the one carrying the thread for the people around you, and you call it just what you do.
cells.ask: Tell one person what it costs you to carry what you carry for them.
cells.core:
You're holding things together for people — a ritual, a tradition, a standard, a way of doing things — and you do it well enough that it looks accidental. It isn't. Nobody's making you do it, but nobody's thanking you for it either, least of all you. When the load is set to carry and you're the one with the hands, that's not a fact of nature. That's a person making a choice about how things go. The people around you don't know that choice is being made. You do.

The weight is real, and it's been real the whole time. What's missing is the saying-so. One sentence to the people who've been benefiting from you, telling them what it takes. Not a confession. Just truth they haven't been told. You built the bridge; you can name it without the naming being about you.
cells.sheetLine: You carry the thread for everyone, and nobody's heard about the weight.
